title: As the Word comes to me, Lalo
word: As the Word comes to me
hook: as the Lord's Word comes to me, so I speak, Lalo (Tilang M1, ang 722)
tomorrow: The one whose head He guards

segments.voice: Yesterday, whatever you ask, and your line: ask your master. What good thing did you ask for? Today the asking stops, and Guru Nanak speaks hard truth to an old friend. Day six hundred fifty-nine.

Early in the path, we met Bhai Lalo, the carpenter of Saidpur, whose plain bread Guru Nanak chose over a rich man's feast. Around 1521, the same town was attacked. Babur's army came down from Kabul, the army that would soon found the Mughal empire in India. Tradition says Guru Nanak was there, and was taken captive for a time. Afterward he sang about what he'd seen. And he addressed the song not to a king, and not to the crowd, but to his friend, the carpenter.
screen: `LALO, THE CARPENTER OF SAIDPUR.` → `AROUND 1521, THE TOWN IS ATTACKED.` → `A SONG TO A FRIEND.`

segments.voice: The shabad is in Raag Tilang, on ang 722. It opens, in effect: as the Master's Word comes to me, so I speak, Lalo. Then it describes the invasion with terrible clarity. The invader came from Kabul like a wedding party of sin, demanding a bride by force. Modesty and righteousness hid themselves; falsehood strutted about as leader. The religious officials of both communities, the qazis and the brahmins, were pushed aside. And the women, the hymn says, women of every community, suffered. Songs of blood were being sung. Two things stand out. First, the courage of it. Guru Nanak names an emperor's violence plainly, while that power was rising over Punjab. He doesn't soften it or flatter it. He says what he saw. Second, why he can. The first line is the key: as the Word comes to me, so I speak. The word is baani, and its root is the same as Gurbani, the Guru's word. Guru Nanak isn't offering his own opinion about politics. He's saying the Word moves through him, and he won't edit it to keep himself safe. That's why the line has become, for Sikhs, a kind of standard for honest speech: say what is true, as it comes, even to power. And notice who he tells it to. Not the emperor's court. Lalo, a working man, a friend. The truth about power is told first to the people who suffer under it. Sikhs hear the shabad as grief, as protest, and as a promise that the Word will not stay silent.
screen: `AS THE WORD COMES, SO I SPEAK.` · `A WEDDING PARTY OF SIN FROM KABUL.` · `SONGS OF BLOOD, PLAINLY NAMED.` · `TOLD FIRST TO A WORKING FRIEND.` · then, large: `AS THE WORD COMES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: speak honestly once. Sit and think of something true you've been holding back: at work, in your family, with a friend. Not a cruel truth, and not a rant. A true one, said with care. Feel how much you've been editing it to keep yourself safe. Now picture saying it plainly, as it comes, to the right person. Notice the fear, and notice what's underneath the fear. If you pray, you can ask the One for courage with a quiet Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
As the Word comes to me. Guru Nanak to Bhai Lalo: as the Master's Word comes, so I speak, even about an emperor's violence.
screen: `AS THE WORD COMES TO ME — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: as the word comes. Today, say one true thing you've been editing, kindly and plainly, to the person who needs to hear it. Day six hundred fifty-nine.

howItsDone: Sikhs sing Guru Nanak's Tilang shabad addressed to Bhai Lalo, one of the hymns known as the Babar Vani, and cite its opening line as a model of fearless, truthful speech.

original.note: Gurmukhi: the Word, speech from the Master; khasam kee baanee, the Master's Word.

trapdoor: what you thought: Guru Nanak commenting on the news.
what it means: the Word speaking through him, unedited, even about an emperor.

what a scholar hears: the Tilang shabad is one of the Babar Vani hymns on the 1520s invasions, a rare eyewitness voice; its opening line grounds prophetic speech in baani rather than personal opinion.

sources.ref: Tilang M1, Ang 722–723 (jaisee mai aavai khasam kee baanee)

notes: Sensitive: the hymn describes violence against women; the script names it without detail. Confirm the handling.
Confirm the date (around 1521) and the tradition that Guru Nanak was taken captive at Saidpur.
Paraphrase covers 'paap kee janj lai kaabaloh dhaaiaa', 'saram dharam doe chhap khaloe, koorr phirai pardhaan', the qazis and brahmins set aside, and 'khoon ke sohile gaaveeah'; confirm.
Babur's faith is not mentioned, to avoid making a tradition the foil; the hymn itself sets aside officials of both communities.
